stem:
The following data relate to three commodities P, Q, and R. Compute the Paasche Price Index for the current year.

Commodity | Base price (p0) | Current price (p1) | Current quantity (q1)
P         | 40              | 50                 | 10
Q         | 50              | 60                 | 20
R         | 60              | 66                 | 30

per_option_rationale.rationale: Used base-year quantities (q0) instead of current-year quantities as weights, computing the Laspeyres index: if q0 = 30, 20, 10 respectively, Laspeyres = (50*30+60*20+66*10)/(40*30+50*20+60*10)*100 = 3360/2800*100 = 120.0. Confusing Paasche with Laspeyres is the primary trap.
Computed the simple (unweighted) arithmetic mean of price relatives: (50/40 + 60/50 + 66/60)/3 * 100 = (1.25+1.20+1.10)/3 * 100 = 3.55/3 * 100 = 118.3. This ignores quantity weights entirely.

A computation slip in one of the products, for example misreading 66*30 as 66*20=1320 instead of 1980, giving sum p1*q1 = 3020 and sum p0*q1 = 2200 and an index near 137 or alternatively misreading q1 for R as 10 and getting (500+1200+660)/(400+1000+600)*100 = 2360/2000*100 = 118, close to 110 with further slip.

explanation: Paasche Price Index uses current-year quantities as weights throughout. sum p1*q1 = 500+1200+1980 = 3680; sum p0*q1 = 400+1000+1800 = 3200; Paasche = 3680/3200 * 100 = 115.0.

explanation_sections.punchline: Paasche uses current-year quantities (q1) as weights; Laspeyres uses base-year quantities (q0). Swapping them changes the answer from 115 to 120 here.
explanation_sections.approach: Name the formula: P_Paasche = (sum p1*q1)/(sum p0*q1)*100. Map givens: three commodities, use q1 throughout. Row by row: P: p1*q1=500, p0*q1=400; Q: p1*q1=1200, p0*q1=1000; R: p1*q1=1980, p0*q1=1800. Totals: 3680 and 3200. Index = 3680/3200*100 = 115.0.
explanation_sections.lesson: The Paasche index anchors on current demand patterns (q1); the Laspeyres on past demand (q0). Paasche tends to be lower than Laspeyres when consumers substitute away from expensive goods, as they do here.
explanation_sections.timing: 80-90 s. Six multiplications then two sums then one division. Double-check which quantity set to use before computing.
